overview: Hamburg was a self-governing trading city on the Elbe, with a powerful merchant elite and a much larger population of working families. This entry follows its eighteenth- and nineteenth-century free-city history. The map’s 1715 to 1878 span is only a display interval: French rule interrupted its autonomy, and Hamburg continued after 1878.

sections.title: A city governed by citizens, but which citizens?

items.text: After French rule, Hamburg regained its place as a free city and became a founding member of the German Confederation in 1815. Much of the earlier governing order returned. Officials even abandoned the French civil registers in favor of church records again, showing that restoration reached into how families’ births and marriages were recorded.

Writing sample: Article 6 of the 1860 constitution says, “Die höchste Staatsgewalt steht dem Senate und der Bürgerschaft gemeinschaftlich zu.” This means, “The highest state authority belongs jointly to the Senate and the citizens’ assembly.” The German wording survives in the constitutional text, reproduced in a scholarly edition with its historical spelling.

The new constitution did not give every adult an equal vote. One group of representatives was elected by qualifying male citizens who paid tax; other seats involved property owners and selected bodies. Women were excluded. The elaborate rules help explain how merchant and established civic interests retained influence even after reform.

sections.title: A small home with a shared courtyard

items.text: The grocers’ guild built homes for twenty members’ widows in 1676, before this map interval, and the houses remained in use through the nineteenth century. Support for older women also freed shop premises for new guild members. This was organized retirement housing for a particular occupational community, rather than help available to everyone.

Each widow’s narrow home had rooms on two levels. The cramped kitchen received daylight through an internal window, while the upstairs living room included an enclosed sleeping alcove. Today’s museum furniture comes from other nineteenth-century Hamburg grocers’ households, so it illustrates that living environment rather than preserving one resident’s untouched possessions.

The widows shared a toilet at the end of the courtyard and used two water pumps until pipes arrived late in the nineteenth century. Wood and peat could be brought through a loft opening. Getting water, fuel and a little privacy all required more movement around the courtyard than turning a modern tap.

sections.title: Fire, water and the problem of clean streets

items.text: From 5 to 8 May 1842, fire spread through central Hamburg. Inadequate supplies of firefighting water helped turn a blaze into a disaster. Rebuilding became an opportunity to change streets and infrastructure, while engineer William Lindley helped design a more coordinated system for supplying the city with water.

Hamburg’s first modern sewer, locally called a Siel, went into service in 1843. Lindley planned drainage that flowed downhill under gravity, together with water supply and hydrants for firefighters. The Rothenburgsort waterworks began supplying water in 1848. These were connected pieces of infrastructure, not simply a taller public fountain.

Piped water did not automatically mean safely filtered water. Hamburg’s centralized supply began in 1848, but the Kaltehofe sand-filtration works did not provide filtered drinking water until 1893, after this entry’s map interval. That gap is a useful reminder that delivering water and cleaning it are separate engineering jobs.

Charlotte Paulsen’s association created childcare institutions for working mothers and a school for poor girls. The children were meant to receive education and encouragement, not merely supervision. In 1866 these efforts came together in the Paulsenstift, which also offered training for girls leaving school.

Johanna Goldschmidt founded Hamburg’s Fröbel association in 1860 to train kindergarten teachers professionally. Education became a field in which women organized institutions and pursued skilled work. The same movement had to overcome expectations that a girl’s future marriage made serious vocational education unnecessary.

The Sandtorhafen, developed in the mid-1860s, brought quays, storage sheds and railway access together at a new harbor basin. Cranes and specialized teams changed loading and unloading. A cargo’s journey increasingly linked ship, quay, warehouse and train, although difficult manual work remained part of port life.

Even after the old fortifications were dismantled, gates and barriers controlled movement into Hamburg. Tolls helped collect city duties and limit outside goods. These restrictions lasted until the turn of 1860 to 1861. Street names associated with old barriers preserve traces of a city where an evening journey could involve a gate and a fee.

A municipal report published in 1887 looks back on the arrival of gas street lighting. An 1845 trial was interrupted when storm flooding damaged the gasworks; regular service began in September 1846. By that year’s end, the account lists 2,020 gas lamps. Lighting streets required pipes, fuel and maintenance behind every flame.

ending.text: Hamburg became a constituent state of the German Empire in 1871. Its trading city and civic institutions continued beyond the imported map’s 1878 endpoint, although wider German political changes repeatedly altered their powers. The endpoint does not represent a conquest or the abandonment of the city.
